description: Surfactant protein C is made by alveolar type II cells as a propeptide that must fold, traffic through the secretory pathway and be proteolytically trimmed before the mature hydrophobic peptide joins the lipid film that lowers surface tension and keeps alveoli from collapsing at end-expiration. Mutations that disrupt folding, routing or processing of pro-SFTPC produce a dominant disease mechanism in which the misfolded proprotein is retained in type II cells rather than simply being absent. The retained precursor triggers endoplasmic reticulum stress, reactive oxygen species generation and autophagy, injuring and killing the cells that renew the alveolar epithelium. The result is impaired surfactant homeostasis with floccular material filling alveoli, seen as interstitial lung disease and as respiratory distress in newborns.

Purine nucleoside phosphorylase normally strips the sugar from inosine, deoxyinosine, guanosine and deoxyguanosine, releasing hypoxanthine or guanine for salvage back into nucleotides and clearing the products of nucleic acid turnover. When the enzyme is defective, this phosphorolysis step fails and its substrates build up; deoxyguanosine is rephosphorylated to dGTP, which poisons ribonucleotide reductase and blocks DNA synthesis in dividing cells. T lymphocytes, with their high deoxynucleoside kinase activity and demanding proliferative programme, are the most vulnerable, so loss of activity produces a profound T cell deficiency with variable B cell involvement, recurrent infection, and in many patients neurological impairment and autoimmunity. The disorder sits alongside adenosine deaminase deficiency as an inborn error of purine catabolism causing combined immunodeficiency, and illustrates how a single salvage reaction supports lymphoid development.

Ornithine transcarbamylase performs the second step of the urea cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, condensing ornithine with carbamoyl phosphate to form citrulline and thereby committing waste nitrogen to disposal as urea. Amino acid substitutions in the main chain of the enzyme underlie ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, the most common inherited urea cycle disorder and the only X-linked one. When the enzyme cannot process carbamoyl phosphate, ammonia accumulates in blood, producing encephalopathy, cerebral oedema, coma and death in severely affected newborns. Mutations fall along a severity gradient: those striking catalytic or substrate-binding residues abolish activity and present neonatally, while changes at surface or domain-interface positions leave partial function and surface later, often triggered by protein load, illness or catabolic stress. The pathway connects hepatic nitrogen handling to neurological health, and management relies on nitrogen scavengers and dietary protein restriction.

Alveolar macrophages clear and recycle pulmonary surfactant, and they depend on GM-CSF signalling through a receptor built from an alpha subunit (CSF2RA) and a shared beta subunit (CSF2RB) to acquire that capacity. Loss-of-function mutations in the beta subunit cause pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction 5, also called hereditary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, in which macrophages fail to take up and degrade surfactant lipid and protein; the alveoli fill with floccular surfactant material, gas exchange deteriorates, and respiratory failure follows. The surfactant components involved here — the hydrophobic proteins SFTPB and SFTPC, the collectins SFTPA1, SFTPA2 and SFTPD, and SFTA3 — are secreted by type II pneumocytes to lower alveolar surface tension and support innate defence, then internalised by macrophages via clathrin-coated vesicles. The pathway therefore links haematopoietic cytokine signalling to lung lipid homeostasis rather than to surfactant synthesis itself.

Leucine catabolism proceeds through a mitochondrial flavoenzyme, isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase, which dehydrogenates isovaleryl-CoA to 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA while reducing FAD; loss of this single step causes isovaleric acidemia, one of the classic organic acidemias. Blocked flux backs up isovaleryl-CoA, which is diverted into isovaleric acid, 3-hydroxyisovalerate, isovalerylglycine and isovalerylcarnitine that accumulate in blood and urine and give affected infants the characteristic odour of sweaty feet. Presentation ranges from neonatal metabolic crisis with vomiting, lethargy, acidosis, hyperammonaemia and seizures to a milder intermittent or nearly asymptomatic course, with poor correlation between mutation and severity. Because the defect lies in branched-chain amino acid breakdown feeding acetyl-CoA into the citric acid cycle, catabolic stress and protein load provoke decompensation, and management rests on leucine restriction plus glycine and carnitine conjugation to clear the accumulated acyl groups.

Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 catalyses the first and rate-limiting step of the urea cycle in the liver mitochondrial matrix, condensing ammonia, bicarbonate and two ATP into carbamoyl phosphate so that waste nitrogen can be disposed of as urea. Loss-of-function variants in CPS1 cause an autosomal recessive deficiency in which ammonia accumulates, presenting as catastrophic neonatal hyperammonaemia or as later crises provoked by catabolic stress, infection or protein load; untreated episodes produce cerebral oedema and irreversible neurological injury. The enzyme requires allosteric activation by N-acetylglutamate, so truncating mutations upstream of the C-terminal activator-binding domain abolish activity, while missense changes in the bicarbonate and carbamate phosphorylation domains or the integrating domain that channels carbamate between active sites destabilise folding and reduce catalysis. Severity tracks with residual activity, linking this single enzymatic step to whole-body nitrogen homeostasis.

Adenosine deaminase converts adenosine and deoxyadenosine to inosine and deoxyinosine, the committed step that lets cells dispose of purine nucleosides through the salvage and degradation route toward uric acid. When ADA activity is lost, this deamination step fails and the unprocessed substrates accumulate, with deoxyadenosine being phosphorylated to dATP that poisons ribonucleotide reduction and DNA synthesis. Developing thymocytes and lymphocytes are the cells least able to tolerate this, so the consequence of defective (deoxy)adenosine deamination is severe combined immunodeficiency, with profoundly reduced T, B and NK cells, recurrent infection from infancy, and additional skeletal, neurological and pulmonary features reflecting the enzyme's ubiquitous expression. The disorder is treatable by enzyme replacement, transplantation or gene therapy, making it a model for how a single metabolic clearance reaction sustains adaptive immunity.

Nitrogen from amino acid breakdown leaves the body as urea, and the urea cycle only runs if its first enzyme is switched on by an allosteric activator. N-acetylglutamate synthase makes that activator in the mitochondrial matrix, condensing acetyl-CoA with glutamate to give N-acetylglutamate, the obligatory cofactor of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I. Loss-of-function variants in NAGS abolish activator production, so carbamoyl phosphate is never formed and the cycle cannot begin. The result is N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency, a rare recessive urea cycle disorder presenting with hyperammonemia, vomiting, lethargy, seizures and encephalopathy, often in the newborn period, with low citrulline and risk of permanent neurological damage or death if untreated. It is distinctive among urea cycle defects in responding to carbamylglutamate, a stable analogue of the missing activator that restores flux.

The branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex commits leucine, isoleucine and valine to oxidative breakdown, and mutations that destroy the integrity of its E2 core subunit cause the maple syrup urine disease subtype known as MSUD2. The complex is built from E1 decarboxylase subunits, the dihydrolipoyl transacylase E2 component encoded by DBT, and the shared E3 dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase; E2 carries the lipoyl groups that accept the acyl intermediate and pass reducing equivalents on, so loss of functional DBT stalls the whole complex regardless of intact E1. Branched-chain amino acids and their ketoacids then accumulate in blood, urine and brain, producing the characteristic sweet-smelling urine, encephalopathy, ketoacidosis and risk of cerebral oedema. Management relies on dietary restriction of these amino acids, placing this step at the centre of branched-chain amino acid catabolism and nitrogen handling.

Branched-chain amino acids from dietary protein are disposed of by oxidative decarboxylation of their ketoacid derivatives, a committed and irreversible step performed by the mitochondrial branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex built from BCKDHA and BCKDHB (E1), DBT (E2) and the shared DLD (E3). The products feed acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA into the citric acid cycle, and when the complex fails, leucine, isoleucine and valine and their ketoacids accumulate to neurotoxic levels, producing the encephalopathy, ketoacidosis and characteristic sweet-smelling urine of maple syrup urine disease. Complex activity is switched off by inhibitory phosphorylation of the E1 beta subunit and switched back on by the mitochondrial phosphatase PPM1K, which removes that mark. A frameshift truncating PPM1K destabilises the phosphatase, leaves the dehydrogenase locked in its phosphorylated inactive state, and causes a mild, variant form of the disease that is corrected by restoring wild-type phosphatase.

Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase is the shared E3 subunit of three mitochondrial alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complexes, so recessive loss-of-function mutations in it disable branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and pyruvate dehydrogenase at once. The resulting deficiency presents with lactic acidosis, accumulation of pyruvate, branched-chain amino acids and urinary alpha-keto acids, and progressive neurological deterioration, sometimes with liver involvement. Because the branched-chain complex is affected, the condition is classed with maple syrup urine disease, but its pleiotropic biochemistry sets it apart from defects in the complex's own catalytic subunits, the E1 alpha and beta chains and the E2 transacylase. Mechanistically the E3 component reoxidizes the lipoamide arm after decarboxylation, passing electrons to NAD+; without it, oxidative decarboxylation stalls and both amino acid catabolism and entry of carbon into the citric acid cycle fail. Compound heterozygosity is common and residual activity predicts severity poorly.

Leucine breakdown in mitochondria passes through a biotin-dependent carboxylation step, and loss of that step defines 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency, the most common organic aciduria found by newborn screening at roughly one in 50,000 births. The enzyme converts 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA to 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA as the fourth reaction of leucine catabolism, and is built from an alpha subunit encoded by MCCC1, which carries a covalently attached biotin needed for ATP-dependent carboxylation, and a beta subunit encoded by MCCC2, which supplies carboxyltransferase activity. Recessive mutations in either subunit destabilise the complex, impair catalysis, or block biotinylation, so leucine-derived intermediates spill over into 3-hydroxyvaleric acid and 3-methylcrotonylglycine. Outcomes vary widely: most affected individuals remain mildly affected or asymptomatic, while a small fraction present in the neonatal period with metabolic decompensation and severe neurological injury.

Surfactant protein B is a small hydrophobic peptide, cleaved from a larger precursor in alveolar type II cells, that lets phospholipid films spread across the air-liquid interface and lowers surface tension so alveoli do not collapse at end-expiration. When SFTPB is mutated, the mature peptide is lost and the pathway of surfactant assembly fails at two points: lamellar bodies form abnormally and the SFTPC precursor is left partially processed and inactive, so floccular lipoprotein material accumulates in air spaces instead of a functional film. The result is pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction type 1, a rare disorder of surfactant homeostasis, and a severe respiratory distress syndrome that presents in newborns and premature infants and is typically fatal without transplantation. This biology links intracellular processing of a secreted proprotein to alveolar mechanics and neonatal lung function.

Argininosuccinate lyase performs the fourth step of the urea cycle, splitting argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate so that waste nitrogen can be disposed of as urea and so that the cycle's arginine supply is regenerated. Loss-of-function variants in the gene encoding this homotetrameric enzyme cause argininosuccinic aciduria, a recessive urea cycle disorder in which argininosuccinate accumulates and ammonia is not cleared. Severe neonatal presentations bring hyperammonemia, encephalopathy and respiratory alkalosis, while milder late-onset disease may declare itself only under catabolic stress or infection. Because the active site is formed at subunit interfaces, different mutant alleles can partially complement one another within a tetramer and leave residual activity, which helps explain the wide clinical spectrum. Beyond ammonia detoxification, the reaction also supplies arginine for nitric oxide synthesis, a likely contributor to the hypertension and neurological features seen in patients.

Alveolar macrophages clear and recycle pulmonary surfactant, and they can only do so when GM-CSF signalling licenses their maturation and catabolic function. The receptor is a heterodimer of a ligand-binding alpha subunit and a shared signalling beta subunit; loss-of-function mutations in the alpha subunit gene block this input, so surfactant lipids and the surfactant proteins A, B, C and D accumulate in alveoli instead of being taken up and degraded. The resulting disorder, pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction type 4 or hereditary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, fills airspaces with floccular lipoproteinaceous material and impairs gas exchange, presenting as progressive hypoxaemic lung disease in children. The same surfactant components maintain alveolar surface tension and innate defence, so their mishandling links macrophage growth-factor signalling to respiratory failure, with misfolded proprotein forms provoking ER stress, oxidative stress and autophagy in alveolar epithelium.

Ornithine transcarbamylase catalyses the second step of the urea cycle inside mitochondria, condensing carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to make citrulline so that waste nitrogen can be disposed of as urea. The enzyme is encoded in the nucleus and made on cytosolic ribosomes, so it must be imported: a 33-residue N-terminal leader sequence directs the precursor across the mitochondrial membranes and is proteolytically removed on arrival. Variants that alter this leader are a recognised cause of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, the most common inherited urea cycle disorder and X-linked in inheritance. Such mutations can destabilise the transcript, lower protein levels, and prevent correct mitochondrial targeting and maturation, leaving the mature enzyme absent from the matrix. The result is hyperammonaemia with orotic aciduria, and in severe neonatal presentations encephalopathy, illustrating how a failure of protein targeting alone can disable an entire metabolic route.

Argininosuccinate synthase carries out the third step of the urea cycle, joining citrulline to aspartate in an ATP-dependent condensation to form argininosuccinate, and it is the point at which loss-of-function variants produce type 1 citrullinemia. The enzyme works in the cytosol of hepatocytes, with lower activity in kidney, and its output feeds both nitrogen disposal as urea and the endogenous supply of arginine for downstream uses such as nitric oxide synthesis. Missense changes typically destabilise folding or the citrulline and aspartate binding sites, while nonsense, frameshift and splice-site variants remove the protein altogether; the common G390R allele is recurrent among more than a hundred catalogued mutations. The result is hyperammonemia with raised plasma citrulline, glutamine and orotic acid and low arginine, and in severe neonatal presentations lethargy, vomiting, seizures, coma and death from ammonia-driven encephalopathy.

Short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase deficiency is an inborn error of mitochondrial metabolism caused by loss-of-function mutations in ECHS1, the hydratase that adds water across the double bond of short-chain enoyl-CoA intermediates. The enzyme serves two converging routes: the hydration step of mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation, and the degradation of branched-chain amino acids, where its preferred substrate is the valine-derived methylacrylyl-CoA and it also acts on the leucine intermediate 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA while binding but barely turning over the isoleucine-derived tiglyl-CoA. When the enzyme is absent, reactive methylacrylyl-CoA and related acyl-CoA species accumulate and damage mitochondrial proteins, producing a Leigh-like encephalopathy with basal ganglia lesions, epilepsy, cardiac involvement and severe developmental and neurological regression. The disorder illustrates how a single hydratase step links amino acid catabolism to cellular energy supply and to metabolite detoxification in the brain.

Adenine released by polyamine synthesis and nucleic acid turnover is normally recycled rather than degraded, and adenine phosphoribosyltransferase performs that salvage step by transferring a phosphoribosyl group from PRPP onto free adenine to give AMP. When the enzyme is defective, this purine salvage route fails and adenine is instead oxidised by xanthine dehydrogenase to the highly insoluble metabolite 2,8-dihydroxyadenine, which precipitates as crystals in urine and renal tissue. The clinical consequence is APRT deficiency: radiolucent kidney stones, crystalline nephropathy, and progressive renal failure that can recur after transplantation unless xanthine oxidoreductase is inhibited. The biology sits within purine metabolism, where salvage pathways spare the energetic cost of de novo nucleotide synthesis, and it illustrates how loss of a single recycling enzyme causes disease through toxic accumulation of the unsalvaged substrate rather than through nucleotide shortage.

Alveolar type II cells recycle phosphate from the airspace for surfactant synthesis, and they do so through the sodium-dependent phosphate cotransporter NaPi-2b encoded by SLC34A2, which moves divalent phosphate across the apical membrane together with three sodium ions in an electrogenic step driven by the sodium gradient. The same transporter operates, less abundantly, in intestinal, pancreatic, prostatic and renal epithelia, where it contributes to dietary and systemic phosphate handling. When SLC34A2 function is lost, phosphate liberated in alveolar fluid is no longer cleared and precipitates with calcium as microscopic calcium phosphate concretions, producing pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis. Affected individuals are often asymptomatic for years before a slowly progressive decline in gas exchange and lung compliance, which can end in respiratory failure. This links a single epithelial transport activity to surfactant metabolism and to the prevention of ectopic mineralisation in the lung.

Branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine and valine are degraded by a mitochondrial multienzyme complex whose first, committed step is oxidative decarboxylation of their transaminated keto acids. That reaction is carried out by the E1 heterotetramer built from BCKDHA and BCKDHB subunits docked onto the DBT transacylase core. Severe loss-of-function mutations in either E1 subunit disrupt subunit interfaces or the hydrophobic core, so the complex fails to assemble and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase activity is lost. Branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids then accumulate in blood, urine and brain, producing classic maple syrup urine disease with its characteristic sweet-smelling urine, neonatal encephalopathy, cerebral oedema and, untreated, death; management depends on lifelong dietary restriction. Mutations at BCKDHA define MSUD type 1A and those at BCKDHB type 1B, the latter accounting for roughly a third of cases.

Purine bases released by nucleic acid turnover are normally recycled rather than discarded, and hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase is the enzyme that does it, transferring a phosphoribosyl group from PRPP onto hypoxanthine to make IMP and onto guanine to make GMP. Loss of this salvage activity forces the cells to depend entirely on energetically costly de novo purine synthesis, while the unsalvaged bases are oxidized by xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase to urate. The consequences in humans are striking: partial deficiency produces gout and urate nephropathy from overproduction, and near-complete deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan disease, with hyperuricaemia, dystonia, cognitive impairment and compulsive self-injurious behaviour reflecting the particular reliance of basal ganglia dopaminergic neurons on purine recycling. The pathway links nucleotide economy to neurodevelopment and to renal handling of uric acid.

Loss of branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase kinase activity leaves the cell unable to brake catabolism of leucine, isoleucine and valine, and the resulting shortage of these amino acids causes a neurological disorder with impaired intellectual development, microcephaly and autistic features. Normally the kinase phosphorylates serine residues on the E1 alpha subunit of the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, switching off the irreversible oxidative decarboxylation step that commits branched-chain ketoacids to degradation; this sets how much of the dietary supply is spared for protein synthesis and neurotransmitter-related metabolism. When the kinase is inactivated, the complex, built from the E1 alpha and beta subunits with the E2 transacylase and the shared E3 dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase, runs unrestrained, and branched-chain amino acids fall in plasma, tissue and urine. It is the mirror image of maple syrup urine disease, and symptoms respond to dietary branched-chain amino acid supplementation.

Beta-ketothiolase deficiency, also called alpha-methylacetoacetic aciduria, is an inherited error of branched-chain amino acid and ketone body metabolism caused by loss of the mitochondrial enzyme ACAT1. Normally ACAT1 performs the thiolytic cleavage of 2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA into propionyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA, the final step of isoleucine catabolism, and also handles acetoacetyl-CoA during ketone body utilisation. Mutations that destabilise the protein or abolish its activity cause isoleucine intermediates and their organic acid derivatives to accumulate in blood and urine, the diagnostic hallmark. Affected children typically present between six and eighteen months with ketoacidotic crises, vomiting, lethargy and occasionally coma, often provoked by infection or fasting; neonatal onset is unusual. As in other branched-chain metabolic disorders, genotype predicts severity poorly, and management rests on avoiding catabolic stress.

Alveoli stay open at the end of each breath because type II epithelial cells secrete a phospholipid-rich surfactant that lowers surface tension, and ABCA3 is the lipid transporter that loads that material into lamellar bodies, the secretory organelles from which surfactant is released. It moves phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylglycerol, the dominant surfactant lipids, from the endoplasmic reticulum membrane into the limiting membrane of the lamellar body, where they are packaged with the surfactant proteins. When ABCA3 is defective, lamellar bodies fail to mature and surfactant is deficient or abnormal, producing pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction type 3: fatal respiratory distress in full-term newborns in severe cases, and chronic childhood interstitial lung disease in milder ones. This places the transporter at the centre of alveolar lipid handling and neonatal lung function.

The final step of the urea cycle is carried out by cytosolic arginase 1, which hydrolyses L-arginine to urea and L-ornithine, completing nitrogen disposal and regenerating the ornithine that re-enters the cycle. The enzyme is most abundant in liver, with lower activity in kidney and red cells. Loss-of-function variants in ARG1 cause arginase 1 deficiency, or hyperargininemia, an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism in which plasma and cerebrospinal arginine accumulate. Affected children typically present after infancy with progressive spastic paraparesis, developmental regression, seizures and growth failure, a neurological course distinct from the other urea cycle disorders because severe hyperammonemia is uncommon. Treatment relies on protein restriction and nitrogen-scavenging agents. This biology links amino acid catabolism and ureagenesis to arginine availability for nitric oxide and polyamine synthesis.

Surfactant protein A2 is one of the pulmonary collectins secreted by alveolar type II cells into the airway, where it helps organise surfactant lipids at the air-liquid interface, regulates surfactant turnover, and opsonises inhaled microbes for clearance. Mutations that disturb the folding of SFTPA2 prevent its secretion: the misfolded protein is retained in the endoplasmic reticulum rather than reaching the alveolar lumen, so its contribution to surfactant homeostasis is lost and the type II cell bears a chronic burden of unfolded protein. The consequence is familial idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, in which repeated alveolar epithelial injury drives progressive scarring, breathlessness and declining gas exchange, typically fatal from respiratory failure within a few years of diagnosis. This links defective SFTPA2 to alveolar epithelial secretory failure as an initiating event in interstitial lung disease.

Valine breakdown in mitochondria passes through a reactive thioester intermediate, and the loss of the hydrolase that clears it defines 3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA hydrolase deficiency, an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism. HIBCH normally catalyses the fifth step of valine catabolism, hydrolysing 3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA to free 3-hydroxyisobutyrate and coenzyme A so the pathway can continue toward methylmalonate semialdehyde and eventually succinyl-CoA. When the enzyme is defective, the unhydrolysed acyl-CoA accumulates and, like the upstream intermediates that build up in ECHS1 deficiency, behaves as a reactive electrophile that modifies cysteine residues in proteins such as those of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. The clinical result is a Leigh-like encephalopathy: psychomotor regression, developmental delay, neurodegeneration and symmetrical basal ganglia lesions. It illustrates how a single branched-chain amino acid catabolic step protects the brain's energy metabolism from its own intermediates.

Leucine, once its carbon skeleton is broken down, passes through a mitochondrial hydratase step that converts 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA to 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA, feeding the amino acid's carbons into ketone body and acetyl-CoA production. The enzyme AUH carries out this fifth reaction of leucine catabolism, and loss-of-function mutations that destabilise or inactivate it cause the autosomal recessive disorder 3-methylglutaconic aciduria. Blocking the step backs up the pathway, so 3-methylglutaconic acid, 3-methylglutaric acid and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid accumulate and spill into the urine, where they serve as the diagnostic signature. Clinical severity is unpredictable, ranging from an incidental biochemical finding to metabolic acidosis, encephalopathy and coma, a spread that reflects how much residual enzyme activity remains and how heavily a given tissue depends on leucine oxidation for energy.

The urea cycle spans two compartments, so ornithine made in the cytosol must be carried into mitochondria and the citrulline made there must be carried out. SLC25A15 is the mitochondrial inner-membrane antiporter that performs this exchange, and loss-of-function variants in it cause hyperornithinemia-hyperammonemia-homocitrullinuria syndrome. Without transport, ornithine accumulates in the cytosol while the matrix is starved of it, leaving carbamoyl phosphate to condense with lysine into homocitrulline and stalling nitrogen disposal; ammonia rises, producing episodic encephalopathy, protein intolerance, spastic paraparesis and developmental impairment. A related carrier, SLC25A2, overlaps in function and partially buffers the defect, which helps explain the variable age of onset and severity. The biology sits at the intersection of amino acid metabolism, mitochondrial solute transport and detoxification of waste nitrogen, and the resulting disorder is managed like other urea cycle defects.
